1:
The argument assumes past mass extinctions show what will happen after anything we do. A weakens it: a global nuclear holocaust could be unlike any past extinction, so its consequences can't be predicted from the fossil record.
B, D and E don't touch the comparison; C is irrelevant to human-made disasters.
2:
The adviser says governments must act to limit family size to cut energy use. C supports this: many births are unintended, so contraception policy could reduce population without forcing anyone.
A and D point to difficulties; B suggests other solutions; E is irrelevant.
3: The argument jumps from 'agents earn some personalities more than their original activity' to 'talent is no longer rewarded'. It overlooks that performers may still be rewarded for real talent as well — B.
4:
The argument dismisses recycling PET because recycled PET used for food containers is a health risk. That only rules out recycling if PET can't be usefully recycled into something else — D.
A works against landfill; B, C and E are not needed.
5:
The passage says sacking shows integrity and the electorate will value that, which is invaluable for staying in power. So, electorally, it pays to lean towards sacking — A.
D is too strong ('always'); B, C and E go beyond the passage.
6: The argument claims organic sales will continue rising only if people get a health benefit. C shows organic sales rose for 50 years even though (if the review is right) there was no health benefit — so sales don't depend on it.
7:
Adult promotion has failed, and the habit forms between 7 and 14. 'Schools need and should be given money to give children an interest in sport' is the recommendation the argument builds to — C.
A and E are premises; B is an intermediate point; D isn't said.
8:
Reasons: films cost a lot, so filmmakers chase big audiences, producing violent films. 'Therefore, the Government should invest in the film industry' — A is the conclusion.
C is the reason given for it; B, D and E are earlier steps.
9:
The argument says governments wanting more university science students must curb health-and-safety rules that stopped exciting experiments. That assumes exciting lessons lead students to take science further — B.
A, C, D and E are not needed.
10:
After the 1997 ban, firearms crime overall rose 5%. So the law has not reduced gun crime — D.
A assumes cause; B, C and E aren't supported by the figures.
11:
Conclusion: police need more training (because they hold false, evidence-free beliefs). E strengthens it by showing those beliefs cause real problems (more complaints), so fixing them matters.
B weakens; A, C and D don't show more training is needed.
12:
The argument dismisses the alien explanation because a simple human explanation exists. That assumes that, where two explanations compete, we should prefer the ordinary one — A.
B, C and D are stronger than needed; E is not used.
13:
The argument says catalytic converters make people with breathing problems worse off. C weakens it: the pollutants the converters remove also cause breathing difficulties, so removing them helps too.
A, B, D and E don't counter the harm claim.
14: The worry is that the two groups' diets become more similar over time. A adds a second reason for this: control subjects also change towards healthier diets after media reports, so the gap shrinks even faster.
15:
The claim: decline is due to libraries' image, not loss of interest in books, so new-style libraries are the future. C supports that interest in reading continues (bookshop sales rising), so the problem is the libraries.
E weakens; A, B and D don't help.
16:
Everything supports 'we should be grateful that our ancestors discovered how to cook' (energy, digestion, toxins) — C.
A, D and E are reasons; B is a side point.
17:
The argument recommends game for people who care about animal welfare, because factory farming is cruel. That only works if game isn't factory-farmed — C.
A, B, D and E are not needed.
18:
The passage calls prison education funding a disgrace while inmates get internet, TV and gyms. That contrast assumes those facilities have no educational value — B.
A, C, D and E aren't required.
19:
The argument concludes accidents can be cut only by catching and punishing law-breaking drivers. That assumes law-breaking drivers are a significant cause of accidents — C.
E is close but not needed in that form; A, B and D aren't required.
20: The speaker claims more police caused the fall in crime. But crime might have fallen anyway — the link is not shown — C.
21: Science says the batsman lacks time for thought and muscle response, so the argument says science is limited. A weakens this: the response is a learned reflex, not a conscious decision, so science's claim about thinking time doesn't apply.
22:
'This is the exact opposite of what should happen' is the main claim; the rest explains why (dangerous braking, invisible cameras would work better) — B.
D and E are reasons; A and C aren't the point argued.
23:
The writer says Van de Velde's relaxed attitude 'explains fully why the prize eluded him'. That assumes he would have won had winning mattered more — A.
C and E are stronger or different claims; B and D aren't assumed.
24:
Testing was meant to solve drug problems, but it pushed prisoners from cannabis to more harmful heroin. So testing has not solved the drug problem — D.
C is too strong ('cannot'); A, B and E aren't supported.
25: The reasoning builds to 'We must not allow this principle to be abandoned' — B. A is the reason ('our liberty depends on it'); C and E are supporting points; D isn't the argument.
26:
Rearing predator species currently needs wild-caught fish, adding pressure on the oceans. So for now fish farms should avoid them — D.
A, B, C and E go beyond what the passage supports.
27: The argument says marriage makes people wealthier (and happier). E reverses the cause: wealthier people are more likely to marry, so wealth may cause marriage rather than the other way round.
28:
The passage criticises 'doing the right thing' as a sound bite that avoids accountability and is dangerous. The conclusion it points to: politicians should explain their decisions properly — C.
A and E are close but are claims, not the recommendation; B and D aren't supported.
29: The argument says the money should have gone on scholars' conditions. But it also says scholars will come anyway — so spending on them would not bring in money, which was the point of spending — C.
30: The argument blames lack of sunlight for rickets. B weakens it: diet affects vitamin D far more than sunlight, so indoor life may not be the main cause.
